analysis.one_liner: Raises the cap on the federal deduction for state and local taxes from $10,000 to $100,000.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Ways and Means Committee in January 2025 with four Democratic cosponsors; the committee has taken no action and the bill has never had a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law limits how much state and local tax you can deduct on your federal return to $10,000 per household. This bill would lift that ceiling to $100,000, or $200,000 for married couples filing jointly, retroactive to 2024. Because only households with large state and local tax bills hit the current cap, the change would overwhelmingly go to higher-income families in high-tax states like New York and New Jersey. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and has sat there ever since.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households in high-tax states. The current $10,000 cap binds only on people whose state and local tax bills exceed it, which means homeowners with expensive properties and big earners in states like New York, New Jersey, and California. A family paying $60,000 in state and local taxes at a 37% federal rate would save roughly $18,500 a year. State and local governments in those states also benefit, because a federal deduction makes their high taxes easier for residents to absorb.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the deduction cap for state and local taxes from $10,000 to $100,000, and to $200,000 for joint filers, effective for tax years after December 31, 2024.

The current cap applies only to households whose combined state and local tax payments exceed $10,000, so the relief flows to itemizers with large tax bills — disproportionately high earners in high-tax states.

The bill's title frames the change as fixing a 'marriage penalty,' because the current cap gives joint filers no more room than single filers; raising the joint cap to $200,000 doubles their allowed deduction.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses revenue, which must be made up through borrowing, other tax increases, or spending cuts. The benefit is narrowly distributed: most households take the standard deduction and pay less than $10,000 in state and local taxes, so they would gain little or nothing while sharing the cost of the revenue loss.
analysis.who_pays_short: General federal taxpayers and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is concentrated at the top: the households that hit the $10,000 cap are overwhelmingly higher-income itemizers, while most working families see no change in their taxes.

The measure is retroactive to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, which raises its cost and mainly benefits people who have already filed or will file large state and local tax payments for those years.
A larger federal deduction for state and local taxes effectively shifts part of the cost of high state taxes onto federal taxpayers nationwide, including residents of low-tax states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it undoes a cap that hits some filers hard, and it does fix the genuine inconsistency where a joint filer gets no more deduction than a single filer. But the money flows almost entirely to affluent households, and the revenue loss falls on everyone through the deficit or offsets elsewhere. A more targeted fix for the marriage-penalty problem could help far more filers at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in January 2025, and the committee has never scheduled it for consideration.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced the bill on January 7, 2025, the opening day of the 119th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law, on the same day.
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base of five sponsors out of 435 members.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no action taken, the current $10,000 cap stays in place, so the federal Treasury keeps the revenue and the tax code remains as it was. Affluent households in high-tax states continue paying under the cap.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican from a high-tax suburban New York district and all four cosponsors are Democrats, but with only five total sponsors and no votes taken, no party-line pattern has formed.

industries.note: Only households paying more than $10,000 in combined state and local taxes benefit, and those are overwhelmingly affluent itemizers in New York, New Jersey, and California. The tax cut they would receive is paid for by the federal Treasury, spreading the cost across all taxpayers including those who gain nothing.

industries.industry: State and local governments in high-tax states
industries.note: A federal deduction makes high state and local taxes cheaper for affluent residents to bear, giving those governments more room to sustain high tax rates and spending. The offset is a larger federal deficit, which everyone shares.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no committee action since January 2025. SALT relief has support among Republicans from high-tax states, but as a standalone bill it competes with broader tax legislation and faces resistance from members concerned about a tax cut skewed to high earners. The likeliest path is that it stays parked in Ways and Means unless SALT becomes central to a larger tax bill, in which case a smaller compromise (short of $100,000) could be folded into that bill instead.
